Before anything else happens, your prompt gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**. A token is often a whole word, but it can be a chunk of a word or even a single punctuation mark. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these pieces, and every one gets swapped for a number.

[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM works on numbers that stand for pieces of text, not on words the way you read them.[/KEY]

Notice that "bank" gets the same token whether you mean money or a riverbank. The model sorts out which meaning you intend by looking at the other tokens around it.

[Q]
In "I sat on the bank of the river", why can the model tell "bank" doesn't mean a place for money?
A) It gives "bank" a different token number whenever the sentence is about nature
B) The token for "bank" is the same, but nearby tokens like "river" shape how the model interprets it
C) It looks up "bank" in a dictionary and picks the meaning that fits a river
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) The token for "bank" is the same, but nearby tokens like "river" shape how the model interprets it
replies.raw:
Right, B is correct. The token stays the same, and the surrounding tokens do the work of settling the meaning. That's the job of the **attention mechanism**: when the model processes "bank", it weighs how much to focus on each other token in the sentence, so "river" pulls the meaning one way and "cash" pulls it the other.

Now for the part that surprises people: what the model does with all that context is guess the next token.

That's it. Given everything so far, it scores every token in its vocabulary by how likely it is to come next, then picks one. Then it adds that token to the text and repeats, one token at a time, until the reply is done.

[EX]
Look at "The cat sat on the ___". The model's scores might look like this (made-up numbers): "mat" 40%, "floor" 15%, "couch" 10%, "roof" 3%, and the rest spread thinly across everything else.
[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM doesn't look answers up; it scores every possible next token and picks one, over and over.[/KEY]

A) "Twinkle, twinkle, little ___"
B) "She opened the door and saw a ___"
C) "My favorite thing to do on weekends is ___"
ANS: A

replies.raw:
Here's something that surprises most people: an LLM never sees your words. It only sees numbers.

Before your prompt reaches the model, it gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**, and each piece is swapped for a number. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of them.

[KEY]An LLM doesn't read words; it reads a sequence of token numbers.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine the sentence "I put cash in the bank" gets split into tokens like "I", " put", " cash", " in", " the", " bank". Each one becomes a number, say 40, 3139, 8515, 304, 279, 6860 (made-up IDs, since real ones differ between tokenizers).[/EX]

Notice that "bank" gets the same token number whether you mean a river bank or a money bank. The model has to sort out which one you meant from the surrounding tokens.

[Q]
A tokenizer turns "bank" into the same token number in "I sat on the bank of the river" and "I put cash in the bank". What does that tell us?
A) The model is guaranteed to confuse the two meanings
B) The token is just a label, and the surrounding tokens are what let the model work out the meaning
C) The tokenizer secretly looks up the meaning of each word in a dictionary first
ANS: B
[/Q]

Given everything so far, it scores every token in its vocabulary and picks from the likeliest ones. Then it adds that token to the text and repeats, one token at a time.

Here's something that surprises most people: an LLM never sees your words. It sees numbers.

Before anything else happens, your prompt gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**, which are chunks of text, often whole words but sometimes parts of words. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of them, and each token gets swapped for a number.

Take "The cat sat on the mat." The model might see it as something like [464, 3797, 3332, 319, 262, 2603]. (Those ID numbers are made up for illustration; real tokenizers each use their own.)

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.
replies.raw:
You've got it, including the point that splits don't always land on word boundaries. A long or rare word can be broken into several tokens, while a common word like "the" is usually just one.

Here's the next idea. Once your prompt is numbers, the model's whole job is to answer one question: given everything so far, which token is most likely to come next?

Try it yourself: "The cat sat on the ___". Most people think "mat" or "floor" or "couch" right away. The model does the same thing, except it scores every token in its vocabulary and gives each one a probability.

It picks a token, adds it to the text, and asks the question again. That loop is how every response gets written, one token at a time.

This is also why an LLM isn't a search engine. It doesn't look up an answer. It predicts a likely continuation.
